title: 3-Read Friday #123
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's weekly three-link digest, issue 123, gathers a classroom-management post, a school-culture reflection and a maths questioning technique, and in each case Barton supplies his own framing rather than a bare link. His commentary on the first post reframes the familiar cascade of toilet requests as social contagion rather than student avoidance, and points to the counterintuitive fix of answering nonverbally. On the second he reads Lynsey White's start-of-term piece as an argument that culture is carried in micro-moments, not initiatives. On the third he connects Paul Rowlandson's questioning move to variation theory, noting that asking students to predict the effect of a change sharpens the distinctions between superficially similar concepts. The issue's through line is that small procedural and conversational choices carry disproportionate weight, whether the subject is a hall pass, a greeting at the bus, or a tweak to a worked example.
points: Barton's gloss on the restroom post locates the problem in social contagion, arguing that one spoken request pulls the whole room off task.
He flags that the fix comes from the idea of maintaining silence, with the novelty sitting in how the teacher responds rather than in the request itself.
White's piece is presented as a claim about micro-moments, greeting at the bus and knowing a name, rather than about tracking or setting.
Rowlandson's prediction question is framed as a forward-looking use of variation theory that also builds functional thinking.
Barton notes that one of Rowlandson's examples exposes a student method that only arrives at the right answer by accident.
quotes: Can I go to the toilet?”. Every teacher dreads those six words because they know what will follow: three or four other students, all asking the same thing, and before you know it, the lesson turns to chaos.
Ms Sam argues that the familiar cascade of toilet requests is less about students dodging work and more about social contagion. One spoken request pulls everyone’s thinking off the task.
Her fix borrows from the idea of maintaining silence, with a surprisingly simple twist in how the teacher responds.
Lynsey argues that school culture lives in the micro-moments: a greeting at the bus, a teacher knowing your name, an adult stopping for a child who looks lost.
Watching her daughter start Year 7 from the other side of the gate, she makes the case that warmth is far from an optional extra.
Paul recommends asking students to predict the effect of tweaking a question before they answer it. Doing so sharpens distinctions between similar concepts and builds functional thinking.
And one for my fellow maths geeks to finish. If you love variation theory as much as I do, you’re in for a treat.
